chief_complaint: hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis and dull interscapular back pain in patient with 6.5 cm descending aortic aneurysm
hpi_details: 69M presenting with left recurrent laryngeal nerve compression hoarseness and CT showing 6.5 cm saccular aneurysm of descending thoracic aorta undergoing Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR).
ideas: He thinks he has developed throat cancer or vocal cord strain along with an ordinary pulled muscle in his upper back.
concerns: He is worried that an advanced throat tumor will permanently take away his voice and prevent him from speaking with his grandchildren.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will look down his throat with a small camera and prescribe lozenges and anti-inflammatory medicine to restore his voice.

available_results.test: CT angiography of the thoracic aorta
available_results.value: 6.5 cm saccular descending thoracic aortic aneurysm with suitable proximal and distal landing zones for TEVAR; no rupture

clinical_knowledge.topic: Descending Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Descending Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Elective repair (TEVAR preferred over open repair when anatomy is suitable) is generally indicated for descending thoracic aneurysms ≥5.5-6 cm, or smaller if rapidly growing or symptomatic (as with this nerve-compression hoarseness).
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis and dull interscapular back pain in patient with 6.5 cm descending aortic aneurysm

Key HPI features: 69M presenting with left recurrent laryngeal nerve compression hoarseness and CT showing 6.5 cm saccular aneurysm of descending thoracic aorta undergoing Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR).
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Thoracic Descending Aortic Aneurysm TEVAR.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Descending Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vocal cord paralysis from another cause (e.g., lung cancer) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden severe tearing pain — would suggest impending rupture or dissection, a true emergency.
management_principles: Optimize blood pressure control (beta-blockers/ACE inhibitors) and confirm aneurysm size/anatomy with CT angiography
Refer to cardiothoracic/vascular surgery for elective TEVAR given size and symptomatic nerve compression
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A large dilation of the descending thoracic aorta can compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness, along with dull back pain — treated with thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) when large enough.
differentials: Vocal cord paralysis from another cause (e.g., lung cancer)
red_flags: Sudden severe tearing pain — would suggest impending rupture or dissection, a true emergency

must_ask.say: How long have you had this hoarseness?

history.answer: My voice has become very hoarse and weak over the past month, and I have also had this dull ache between my shoulder blades.
The hoarseness started about five weeks ago, and the dull back pain started roughly four weeks ago.
It started gradually, but my voice has become steadily weaker and more raspy over the last couple of weeks.
It sounds weak, breathy, and raspy, as if air is leaking out whenever I speak.
No, I have not been shouting, singing, or straining my voice at all.
No, I have not had a cold, runny nose, sore throat, or fever recently.
No, I don't suffer from heartburn, sour fluid backing up, or any feeling of a lump in my throat.
No, I have not had any shortness of breath or noisy breathing.
Swallowing feels normal, and I don't have any pain when I swallow or any pain going to my ears.
Occasionally I choke or cough a little if I drink water too fast, but I can eat solid food without any trouble.
No, I haven't noticed any lumps or swelling in my neck, and my weight has stayed the same.
No, I don't have a persistent cough, and I have never coughed up any blood.
It is a steady, dull ache right between my shoulder blades; it is not a sudden, sharp, or tearing sensation.
No, I have not had any chest pain, tightness, or pressure in the front.
I have never had surgery on my neck, thyroid, or chest, and I haven't had a breathing tube placed.
No, I haven't had slurred speech, weakness in my face or limbs, hand tremors, or drooping eyelids.
No, I have never used steroid inhalers or asthma sprays.
No, I haven't felt unusually cold, excessively tired, or noticed dry skin.
When the back ache started last month, my doctor ordered a chest CT scan, and they found a 6.5-centimeter bulge in my descending thoracic aorta.
I have had high blood pressure for about ten years, which my doctor has been treating with daily medication.

I figured I probably developed a growth or cancer on my vocal cords, and just strained a muscle between my shoulder blades from yard work. I'm really worried that it's throat cancer and that I'll lose my voice for good and never be able to talk to my grandkids again.
I was hoping you could check my throat with a small scope today and prescribe some anti-inflammatory medicine to bring my voice back.
Aside from high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol, I have had no other medical conditions.
I had an appendectomy when I was a teenager, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure.
I take a standard daily multivitamin occasionally, but no other supplements or regular painkillers.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products in my life.
I drink an occasional glass of red wine on weekends, but I do not drink heavily.
I am a retired accountant living at home with my wife, and I stay active with daily walking.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke, but no one in my family had an aneurysm.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/86 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius.
Alert, oriented, and in no acute distress; speech is noticeably breathy and hoarse, with no audible stridor or work of breathing at rest.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink without mucosal erythema, tonsillar enlargement, ulceration, or pharyngeal exudate.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is non-tender, normal in size and consistency, with no palpable nodules or bruits.

Bilateral symmetric elevation of the soft palate, uvula is midline, and tongue protrudes midline without fasciculations or atrophy; voice demonstrates a breathy, raspy dysphonia consistent with unilateral vocal cord paresis.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds; no wheezing, rhonchi, crackles, or inspiratory stridor.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs auscultated.
Bilateral radial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ and symmetric without delay between upper and lower extremities.
No spinal tenderness to percussion over the cervical, thoracic, or lumbar vertebrae; no paraspinal muscle spasm.
